issues.legal_issue: A settlor cannot exercise a power to alter beneficial interests by an irrevocable deed when the trust instrument permits alteration only by will.
material_facts: The trust instrument reserved to the settlor the power to vary beneficiaries’ interests after his death by will alone and in no other way.
The settlor later executed an irrevocable deed that altered the beneficiaries’ interests and deprived one beneficiary of an interest in the trust corpus.
issues.conclusion: The restriction to variation by will was a material and binding condition; the settlor had no power to vary that condition or to make the change by deed inter vivos, so the later deed was ineffective.
issues.legal_principle: Equity may relieve against defects in the mode of exercising a power only when the defect is not material to the donor’s intention. It will not give effect to an irrevocable deed under a power exercisable only by will. The Court applied Re Anstis, Reid v. Shergold (1805) 10 Ves. 370, and Molineux v. Evered (1910) 2 Ch. 147, and referred to Halsbury’s Laws of England, 3rd Ed., Vol. 30, para. 518, and Hanbury’s Modern Equity, 7th Ed., p. 56.

predicates.trust_settlement_dispute: The case concerns the terms or administration of a trust settlement.
predicates.power_limited_to_will: The trust instrument permits the settlor to change beneficial interests only by will.
predicates.change_made_by_irrevocable_deed: The settlor attempted to change beneficial interests through an irrevocable deed.

issues.definition: When a trust dispute concerns a power limited to exercise by will and the settlor instead makes an irrevocable deed, the settlor had no authority to make that change.

issues.legal_issue: A court lacks jurisdiction to authorize a substantive alteration of a trust’s beneficial interests when its authority extends only to trust administration.
material_facts: An originating summons sought permission to revoke the term limiting changes to a will and to authorize changes to beneficiaries’ interests by deed inter vivos.
The court order granted those requests as well as appointing a replacement trustee.

The powers invoked or considered by the Supreme Court authorized directions about trust management or administration, or the appointment of a trustee, but did not authorize the requested alteration of beneficial interests; the court’s inherent jurisdiction was also limited.
issues.conclusion: The court had no competence to grant the requested alteration of beneficial interests. Its order granting that relief was void, not merely erroneous or illegal.
issues.legal_principle: Jurisdiction requires authority not only to entertain a matter but also to decide the particular issue and make the order sought. Sections 34 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, and 43 of the Trustees and Mortgagees Powers Act, 1866, permit opinions, advice, or directions on trust management or administration, not alteration of beneficial interests. Section 10(1) of the Official Trustees Act, 1913, could support appointing the Official Trustee but not the other relief. Chapter XIII of the Original Side Rules supplied no authority for that relief, and the inherent equitable jurisdiction was limited to trust administration. The Court approved Hirday Nath Roy v. Ramachandra Barna Sarma, referred to Ittavira Mathai v. Varkey Varkey, and relied on Chapman v. Chapman ([1954] A.C. 429; [1953] Ch. 218).

predicates.order_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of an earlier court order.
predicates.application_sought_substantive_trust_var: The application asked the court to change the trust’s beneficial interests rather than merely direct how the trust property should be administered.
predicates.court_authority_confined_to_trust_admini: The court’s available authority extended only to trust administration and did not include the substantive relief requested.

issues.definition: When an order-validity challenge concerns an application for substantive trust variation and the court’s authority was confined to administration, the order is void for lack of jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: An official trustee who merely acted under a court order is accountable as a trustee from the institution of the beneficiary’s suit and may recover costs from the trust estate.
material_facts: The Official Trustee took charge of the trust and distributed income to beneficiaries in accordance with the court order and the later trust deed.
The beneficiary did not appear in the earlier proceeding and did not challenge the later deed during the settlor’s lifetime; the beneficiary first challenged it by filing the suit.
The Official Trustee had carried out the court order and it was not open to him to go behind it.
issues.conclusion: The Official Trustee was not liable as a trustee de son tort and his liability was no greater than that of a trustee. He was required to account from the institution of the suit, not from the date he took charge, and could reimburse himself from the trust funds for costs incurred in the courts.
issues.legal_principle: Where an official trustee merely carries out a court order, it is unjustified to treat him as a trustee de son tort or impose liability greater than that of a trustee. Where the beneficiary had not previously challenged the arrangement and distributions had been made in reliance on the order, accounting from the suit’s institution meets the ends of justice without reopening earlier transactions. The Court also permitted the trustee to reimburse litigation costs from the trust funds.

rule.if: trustee_accounting_claim and official_trustee_followed_court_order and beneficiary_first_challenged_arrangement_in_suit and distributions_made_in_reliance_on_order

predicates.trustee_accounting_claim: The proceeding seeks an account from a person acting as trustee of a trust.
predicates.official_trustee_followed_court_order: The official trustee acted in accordance with a court order and did not depart from it.
predicates.beneficiary_first_challenged_arrangement: The beneficiary did not challenge the arrangement before bringing the suit seeking relief.
predicates.distributions_made_in_reliance_on_order: The trustee distributed trust income to beneficiaries in reliance on the court order.

issues.definition: When an accounting claim concerns an official trustee who followed a court order, the beneficiary first challenged the arrangement in the suit, and distributions were made in reliance on the order, the trustee accounts from the suit and recovers costs from the trust estate.
